obs: Weston and Others v. the City Council of Charleston
"What then is the ordinance in substance % It is a tax upon, the net income of interest... It is the net interest received upon which the tax is laid."

"But the grant to the Pensacola and Louisville Railroad Company by the act of 1872, and that to the Pensacola Railroad Company by the act of 1877, though in form the renewal or transfers of previously existing grants, were in fact the creation of new ones."

"The act of 1860... is retrospective in its form; but its practical agency is to subject to assessment property liable to taxation... and the language retrospective is of no importance, except to describe the property to be included in the assessment."
"It is wholly immaterial what name may be given to it. The fact that it is called a license fee .or franchise .tax cannot validate it. ... it is none the less a tax because it is given a new name."
"It is plainly manifest that no merchant could afford to pay the sum of $6,000 annually for the mere privilege of giving away trading stamps or allowing discount on his cash sales."

"The provisions of the statute referred to in the preceding paragraph of this opinion necessarily condition the tax, however it be characterized. If it be a gift tax, it, nevertheless, is based, not upon the transfer of the gift, but upon the transfer of the estate; and upon the value of the estate, and not that of the gift."

"The question here, then, is, not whether there has been, in the strict sense of that word, a `transfer' ... but whether the death has brought into being or ripened for the survivor, property rights of such character as to make appropriate the imposition of a tax upon that result (which Congress may call a transfer tax, a death duty or anything else it sees fit)"
Stewart Dry Goods Co. v. Lewis

“It is impossible to conceal from ourselves, that this is varying the form, without varying the substance . . . All must perceive, that a tax on the sale of an article, imported only for sale, is a tax on the article itself.”
Liggett & Myers Tobacco Co. v. United States

"If, in reality, the tax was upon the manufacture of tobacco... We think that was the true nature of the exaction"; and "True the limit of time for making payment is when the product is sold or removed, but this is a privilege designed to mitigate the burden; it indicates no purpose to impose the tax upon either sale or removal."
International Harvester Co. v. Wisconsin Department of Taxation
